title: Trump says US carried out minor strikes on Iranian air defences
summary: The president described a short attack on an antiaircraft system after Iranian media reported explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
body:
President Donald Trump has said United States forces carried out what he called minor strikes on Iranian air defences on Friday, hours after Iranian state media reported explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.

Speaking to reporters in West Palm Beach, Florida, Trump said Iranian forces had built a limited antiaircraft device and that American units knocked it out in about 15 minutes, perhaps five. He framed the action as part of a pattern of small strikes rather than a new major campaign.

Iranian state media said the sound of two explosions was heard in the Suza area of Qeshm, a large island that sits on the oil shipping choke point disrupted since the US Iran war began earlier this year. Iran's state broadcaster also aired an army claim that Iranian air defences had intercepted and destroyed an American MQ9 drone over the island. US Central Command, asked about reports of explosions, described the wider situation as relatively calm and declined further public comment.

Friday's action is the first publicly claimed American strike since Republicans suffered a heavy midterm defeat that Trump and other Republicans have linked in part to the Iran war and higher fuel prices. It also follows limited American strikes earlier in the week around Qeshm, Hengam and the nearby mainland near Bandar Abbas that Washington had called defensive.

Diplomatic tracks remain active even as the military signalling continues. Trump said there had been a lot of progress in talks with Tehran, without releasing details of any draft terms. The mix of another limited strike near Hormuz and renewed talk of negotiation keeps markets and regional governments watching whether the week ends in escalation or in a narrower bargaining window.

title: Beijing confirms talks on a historic Xi Trump Putin meeting
summary: China says a three way summit is under discussion while Ukraine faces fresh strikes on Kyiv and presses allies for Patriot missiles and postwar security guarantees.
body:
China has confirmed that it is discussing a historic meeting between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, a format that would place the Ukraine war and great power bargaining on the same stage.

Foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said this week that such a gathering was under discussion. Analysts watching the track say Moscow would likely use any three leader summit to pull Beijing and Washington closer to Russian positions on Ukraine. Advisers around Trump have separately cautioned him against letting Ukraine dominate those talks, according to public briefings circulating after the Chinese remarks.

On the ground the war did not pause for summit talk. Ukraine again came under Russian attack on Saturday. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy repeated calls for allies to supply missiles for US made Patriot batteries to defend Ukrainian cities. Kyiv's mayor reported that an early Saturday missile strike damaged a residential building in the capital, part of weeks of near constant pressure on urban areas and energy sites.

Zelenskyy has also pressed Western partners for specific guarantees on how postwar security support would work once fighting with Russia ends. His comments followed two days of allied discussions in Brussels that brought together officials from the United States, Britain, France, Germany and the European Union, along with the World Bank and a major US investment group, according to Ukraine's lead negotiator.

The diplomatic calendar now holds two competing stories at once: a possible Xi Trump Putin encounter that could redefine leverage over any settlement, and a Ukrainian push for air defence munitions and written security promises before winter deepens the cost of damaged power and housing.

title: US held secret talks with Iran on deporting Iranians amid the war
summary: Court filings show the Trump administration discussed removals through a third country even while calling Tehran an enemy, and a judge ordered advance notice before any deportation.
body:
The Trump administration held secret talks with Iran about deporting Iranians even as the war between the two countries continued, according to court documents unsealed in a US immigration case.

Filings show that as recently as mid October the administration said it had plans to remove Iranians through an unnamed third country, though it was unclear when any such transfers would begin. The case arises from a lawsuit that alleges violations of national immigration rules.

A federal judge ordered the government to give the court 24 hours' notice of any finalised plan to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country, and five days' written notice before carrying out such a removal. During a hearing the judge pressed justice department lawyers on the logic of sending people back to a country the president has described as lawless and as an enemy of the United States, warning of a serious threat of death. The government attorney replied that the United States was executing lawful removal orders.

The disclosure lands while combat and diplomacy with Tehran both remain active, and while Stephen Miller, a chief architect of hardline deportation policy, has just been named White House chief of staff. Public records do not show how many people were targeted, which third country was discussed, or whether Iran agreed to accept returnees. They do show a wartime administration pursuing immigration enforcement against nationals of a state it is fighting, under court supervision that now requires advance notice before any flight.

title: US voters reject data centre projects in almost every midterm ballot fight
summary: Across 41 local measures, communities moved to block or limit large computing sites, with only one small North Dakota town defeating tighter review rules.
body:
American voters used Tuesday's midterm ballots to push back against data centre building, rejecting or limiting projects in nearly every local contest that put the issue to a vote.

An election monitoring project tracked 41 ballot measures tied to data centres across the country. Voters were on course to reject data centre development in all but one of those fights, with two races still being counted but expected to favour limits. The sole clear exception was Harwood, North Dakota, a town of fewer than 800 people, where voters defeated a measure that would have required independent reviews of large industrial projects such as data centres before construction.

The results follow months of local anger over power use, water demand, noise and land consumption linked to the computing halls that train and run artificial intelligence systems. A September poll had found that about 70 percent of respondents opposed new data centres near their communities. Democrats sought to channel that backlash during the campaign, and Tuesday's local tallies suggest the opposition translated into votes even where national party contests dominated headlines.

For the technology industry the message is practical. Expansion plans that assume easy local approval now face a map of hostile ballot outcomes, slower permitting and higher political risk just as investors debate how midterm Democratic gains will shape federal rules on artificial intelligence infrastructure. For residents the votes were often framed more simply as a stand over electricity bills, water and who decides what gets built next door.

title: US measles cases top 5,000, highest tally in 35 years
summary: Health officials report 5,182 confirmed infections, mostly in outbreaks, as kindergarten vaccination coverage slips and children and teenagers account for most cases.
body:
United States health officials have recorded 5,182 confirmed measles cases, the highest national total since 1991, in a surge that is hitting children and teenagers hardest.

Figures released by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show children under five making up 18 percent of cases and those aged five to 19 accounting for 41 percent. Together, children and teenagers represent about 59 percent of confirmed infections. The vast majority, 4,993 cases, were linked to outbreaks rather than isolated introductions.

The climb comes as measles vaccination coverage among kindergarten pupils has fallen from 95.2 percent in the 2019 to 2020 school year to 92.4 percent in 2025 to 2026. Confirmed cases so far in 2026 are more than double the 2,289 recorded across the whole of 2025.

Measles is highly contagious and preventable with routine immunisation. Public health agencies have warned for several years that slipping school entry coverage would reopen gaps large enough for outbreaks to take hold. The latest national count turns that warning into a measured reverse of decades of progress, with families, schools and clinics now managing a disease many American parents had rarely seen.

title: Syrians protest soaring prices as post Assad recovery falters
summary: Fuel rises triggered the largest street anger yet under President Ahmed al Sharaa, testing support two years after the overthrow of Bashar al Assad.
body:
Protests have spread across Syria after another fuel price rise, the clearest show of public anger yet under President Ahmed al Sharaa as living costs climb and the promised recovery after Bashar al Assad fails to arrive for many families.

Last month demonstrators burned tyres, blocked roads and chanted against the latest increase. Television interviews captured supporters of the authorities saying they could no longer afford bread, and others saying they feared what each morning's new decision would bring. The fuel rise was later revoked amid calls for further demonstrations, but it sat on top of a longer run of subsidy cuts and price jumps for essentials.

Sharaa rose to the presidency after rebel forces he led ousted Assad, ending five decades of family rule and more than 13 years of war. The transition was always going to strain a shattered economy after isolation and conflict. Many Syrians nonetheless hoped freedoms would be matched by faster relief on bills and wages. Instead the cost of power, transport and basic goods has kept rising, and some residents complain that visible spending on roundabouts and city projects feels disconnected from household hardship.

The unrest does not yet amount to a full break with the new authorities, and some protesters still say they back the government while rejecting its economic course. It does show that post Assad legitimacy is being tested less on battlefield victory than on whether salaries can buy bread and fuel. How Damascus handles the next subsidy or price decision will shape whether discontent stays on the street or hardens into a lasting political crisis.

title: Ukraine turns attack drones into tools for battlefield rescues
summary: New systems are helping evacuate wounded fighters from ground once written off as unreachable, even as the same machines remain instruments of lethal strikes.
body:
Ukraine is adapting the drone technology that has defined this war's killing power into a means of pulling wounded people out of ground once treated as unreachable.

Public accounts of the new rescue systems describe aircraft and controllers used to locate casualties, drop supplies and support evacuations that earlier required crews to cross fire swept open space on foot or by vehicle. The same platforms that hunt trenches and artillery can now shorten the time between injury and medical care, a change Ukrainian units say matters as much as any incremental gain of territory.

The work is not free of risk. Operators still fly under electronic warfare pressure, hostile fire and weather that can drop a craft or cut a video link mid mission. A failed rescue flight can expose both the casualty and the team trying to help. Commanders weigh those dangers against the certainty that leaving the wounded in place often means death.

The dual use of drones, as hunters and as lifelines, captures the wider character of the war in late 2026. Innovation continues under bombardment of cities and power plants, and every new tool is judged first by whether it keeps soldiers alive long enough to fight another day. Rescue drones will not end the attrition, but they are rewriting what medics and infantry treat as possible on a front where roads and ambulances are often targets.

title: Industries that rely on immigrant labour recoil at Miller's promotion
summary: Employers in sectors dependent on foreign workers voice anger and fear after Trump elevates the architect of hardline deportation policy to chief of staff.
body:
Business leaders in industries that depend on immigrant labour have reacted with anger and alarm to President Donald Trump's decision to make Stephen Miller White House chief of staff.

Miller has been the central designer of the administration's border crackdowns and mass deportation drive. Elevating him to run the West Wing days after a midterm defeat signals that immigration enforcement will stay at the core of the second term agenda even as Democrats prepare to take both chambers of Congress.

Employers in farming, food processing, construction, hospitality and care work have long warned that sudden removals and worksite raids leave shifts unfilled and harvests at risk. Public comments after the appointment described fear of tougher interior enforcement and astonishment that the president chose the hardest line figure available for the most powerful staff job.

The political calculation cuts the other way for Trump's base, which treats Miller as proof that midterm losses will not soften deportation goals. For companies the practical questions are staffing, visas and whether Congress will now fight the White House over funding and oversight of immigration agencies. Miller's promotion turns those questions from a campaign theme into a standing operating risk for any firm that cannot fill jobs without foreign born workers.

title: Midterm shock already reshapes the path to the 2028 White House race
summary: Democrats leave the week with momentum and a crowded field of hopefuls, while JD Vance's blame for the Iran war is read as an early marker for a Republican contest.
body:
Ballots from America's midterm elections are still being counted, yet the political class has already pivoted to the 2028 race for the White House.

Democrats enter that contest with fresh momentum after major gains in Congress. History warns that a strong midterm does not guarantee the presidency two years later. Barack Obama won re election in 2012 after Republicans surged in 2010. Still, the scale of this week's Democratic advance changes fundraising, talent recruitment and the early map of primary states.

No candidate has formally entered the 2028 presidential race, but potential contenders are building staff and testing messages. On the Republican side, Vice President JD Vance's public reckoning with why the midterms went wrong, including his focus on the Iran war, is widely read as preparation for a run. Several politicians who stood in 2026 state and federal races emerged looking stronger and will now face early donor pressure to decide whether to climb higher.

Four early lessons are already circulating among strategists. Midterm winners can lose the next presidential if they overread a protest vote. Foreign wars that dominate one cycle can define the next nominating fight. Party establishments that ignore rising stars in governor and Senate contests risk being outflanked. And the candidate who first owns a clear story about why voters punished Trump's party may set the terms everyone else must answer.

For now the only settled fact is timing. The midterms closed one campaign and opened another before many races finished reporting, pulling Washington's attention from certification fights to the long road toward 2028.

title: Qatar urges US and Iran not to wait for a perfect peace moment
summary: Doha's prime minister says both sides must reach a deal to end the war now, as Iranian state media report missiles striking Qeshm Island without casualties.
body:
Qatar's prime minister has urged the United States and Iran to strike a peace deal without waiting for ideal conditions, as fighting continues and fresh reports emerge of missiles hitting an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz.

Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, who also serves as foreign minister, said during an interview at Oxford University that Washington and Tehran cannot afford to wait for a "perfect moment" to end the war. His appeal frames mediation from Doha as a live option at a time when American politics is still absorbing a midterm defeat widely linked to the conflict, and when Iranian leaders are weighing nuclear and security proposals already circulating in public summaries.

Iran's official news agency IRNA said two missiles struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. Semi official Iranian outlets reported that there were no casualties. The island has featured in earlier American and Iranian claims about limited defensive or retaliatory action, and any confirmed strike near the shipping choke point raises immediate questions for oil transit and regional insurance markets.

The twin messages, a Qatari push for talks and another incident around Hormuz, underline how diplomacy and military signalling are moving in parallel. Public facts do not yet show whether the Oxford remarks were coordinated with Tehran or Washington, or whether the Qeshm reports will harden either side's terms. They do show Doha pressing both capitals to treat a ceasefire window as urgent rather than hypothetical.

title: Midterm sweep deals a blow to Trump's Iran war narrative
summary: America's costliest election still produced a Democratic victory widely read as a rebuke of the conflict, leaving Republicans struggling to regain control of the story.
body:
Republicans poured money into the most expensive midterm contest in American history, yet voters delivered a Democratic sweep that many analysts now cast as a direct rebuke of President Donald Trump's Iran war narrative.

Public tallies put total midterm spending near $12bn, much of it on advertising, with a majority of that money backing Republican candidates. The result was a Democratic victory on a scale not seen in half a century. In the aftermath Trump, long accustomed to turning crisis into political theatre, appeared to lose grip on the story that had framed the campaign.

Coverage of the defeat has linked the repudiation not only to domestic discontent but also to the US Israeli war on Iran. That reading sits beside Trump's own remarks blaming the conflict and higher fuel prices for Republican losses, and beside comments from Vice President JD Vance listing the Israel relationship among reasons voters walked away.

The political meaning is still contested inside the Republican Party, where strategists debate whether to defend the war as unfinished business or to distance the 2028 field from it. What the public record already shows is narrower and harder to spin: a historic spending spree failed to sell the administration's account of the conflict, and Congress now returns with Democrats holding new leverage over war funding, oversight and any settlement track.

title: Hundreds of Palestinian couples marry in a Gaza mass wedding
summary: About 250 couples took part in a shared ceremony organised through a UAE backed humanitarian relief campaign as the war grinds on across the enclave.
body:
About 250 Palestinian couples have married in a mass wedding in Gaza, a public celebration of new family life staged while the war continues to reshape daily existence across the enclave.

Organisers said the event was arranged by Operation Chivalrous Knight, a humanitarian relief campaign backed by the UAE. Couples gathered to exchange vows and mark beginnings that many families have deferred under bombardment, displacement and the collapse of ordinary civilian routines.

Mass weddings have periodically appeared in Gaza during earlier rounds of conflict as a way to cut costs, share scarce resources and assert normal life under abnormal pressure. This gathering stands out for its scale and for the Gulf funding channel named by organisers, at a moment when reconstruction, shelter and basic services remain far short of need.

Public reports do not list individual names, dowry arrangements or whether participants were newly displaced. They do confirm a large, organised ceremony framed as both relief and defiance: a claim that courtship, marriage and family continuity continue even when housing, work and safety do not.

title: Zelenskyy says Russian strikes have damaged every Ukrainian power plant
summary: At a Madrid summit the Ukrainian president pleaded for fast help to repair the grid, saying crews are working around the clock after nationwide energy attacks.
body:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says every power plant in Ukraine has been damaged in one way or another by Russian attacks, and has urged partners to rush equipment for a grid under relentless pressure.

Speaking at a summit in Madrid, Zelenskyy told Latin American leaders that Kyiv needs international cooperation "and we need it fast" to restore electricity infrastructure. He said repair crews were already working around the clock. The appeal lands as winter approaches and as repeated strikes on generation and transmission sites have forced emergency blackouts and industrial slowdowns across the country.

The same public briefing cycle noted continued overnight exchanges of airstrikes, reports of an attack on one of Russia's larger oil refineries, and a Ukrainian strike on a bus in occupied Luhansk that local Moscow backed authorities said killed five people and wounded 13. Those battlefield and energy details sit beside separate diplomacy in Brussels on postwar reconstruction and security guarantees, and beside White House talk of a wider deal with Moscow.

For Ukrainian cities the immediate question is more practical than diplomatic: whether transformers, turbines and spare parts arrive before colder weather multiplies the human cost of damaged plants. Zelenskyy's Madrid message was designed to widen the donor map beyond Europe and North America and to treat power repair as an urgent wartime priority, not a reconstruction task for later.

title: Midterm shock deepens Israeli fears over the US alliance
summary: Israeli leaders and analysts describe a generational shift after Democrats swept Congress and senior Republicans tied losses to Israel and the Iran war.
body:
Israeli assumptions about unshakeable American backing have been jolted by the US midterm results, with politicians and analysts warning of a generational shift in the alliance that long anchored Israel's security planning.

As Democratic victories piled up, Israeli opposition figures blamed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, with one saying the results showed how toxic he had become among Democrats and Republicans alike. A prominent column in a major Israeli daily called the moment a "generational sea change" and said the Netanyahu government had sown the wind and reaped a tsunami. A US official familiar with the debate said Israel's establishment understood intellectually that opinion was moving, but not how far or how fast.

The Iran war and Israel's conduct in Gaza and the occupied West Bank were campaign issues across American races. Trump himself blamed the Iran conflict for the Republican rout, a war Israeli leaders are widely seen as having encouraged. Vice President JD Vance listed the US relationship with Israel among four reasons voters deserted the party, a signal that unsettled Israeli security voices who now fear Republican as well as Democratic pressure.

Shock deepened when Trump said this week that Washington would stop about $3.8bn a year in military aid to Israel by year end, earlier than previously planned. Israel's president called the remark a bolt from the blue. Netanyahu's office later cast a shift from aid toward partnership as proof of strength, but defence analysts noted that American aircraft, spare parts and missile defence supplies remain central to Israeli war planning. A Democrat controlled Congress can slow sales and joint projects even if it lacks the votes to override a presidential veto.

Israeli and American officials still insist the core relationship will endure. Ambassadors on both sides have publicly played down talk of rupture. The midterms nonetheless leave Jerusalem planning for harder scrutiny, slower arms pipelines and less automatic diplomatic cover than Israeli governments treated as routine for a generation.

title: Trump names Stephen Miller White House chief of staff after midterm losses
summary: The hardline immigration adviser will replace Susie Wiles on Monday as Democrats prepare to take both chambers of Congress.
body:
President Donald Trump has named Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff, moving Susie Wiles to his political operation three days after Republicans lost control of Congress.

Trump said on Friday that Miller, one of his closest advisers across both presidential terms, would start on Monday. He thanked Wiles for her service and said she would shift to the Trump Political Operation. Speaking to reporters, he said Wiles had done a very good job but that moves sometimes had to be made.

Miller has been the main architect of the administration's hardline border and deportation policies, a flashpoint in the midterm campaign. He joined Trump's first election team as an adviser in 2016 and stuck with him after the 2020 defeat. Trump called him one of his most trusted advisers and said he understood politics well.

Wiles submitted her resignation on Thursday night after Republicans lost the House and Senate, according to US officials. Three sources said she quit because of the election losses. She described serving as chief of staff as the honour of a lifetime and said her commitment to Trump and the mission would not change even as her role did. Last month Trump had insisted there was zero chance she would be replaced soon.

Democrats are expected to open investigations into Miller once they take control of both chambers in January. House Democrat Robert Garcia, lined up to lead the Oversight Committee, said he would keep probing what he called misconduct linked to immigration raids. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries denounced the appointment in sharp terms.

The shake up comes as other senior figures leave. Justice Department officials including the head of the national security division and a Florida US attorney have resigned in the wake of the midterm rebuke. Trump was widely expected to reshuffle staff after Democrats netted Senate seats and a clear House majority, with some races still being counted.

title: Israel closes Hebron's Ibrahimi Mosque to Palestinians for Jewish holiday
summary: Palestinian worshippers and staff are barred while thousands of Israeli visitors are expected at the contested West Bank holy site through Saturday evening.
body:
Israeli forces have closed the Ibrahimi Mosque in occupied Hebron to Palestinian worshippers as thousands of Israeli settlers gather for a Jewish religious observance.

The Palestinian Ministry of Religious Endowments said worshippers and mosque employees were barred from entering and that the call to prayer had been suspended. The mosque director said Israeli authorities planned to open the prayer halls and courtyards exclusively to Israelis. The closure began on Friday afternoon and is set to last until 10pm on Saturday.

The timing matches an annual Jewish observance linked to Sarah, traditionally believed to be buried at the site with the Prophet Abraham and other family members. Jews know the compound as the Cave of the Patriarchs. Israeli forces said they expected about 20,000 visitors and deployed hundreds of security personnel. Troops tightened checkpoints across Hebron's Old City and restricted some residents from entering or leaving their homes.

Under a 1997 Hebron agreement, Israel held security control of the Old City while the Palestinian municipality kept planning powers. In June, Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich announced a takeover of those planning powers, raising fears of a push toward exclusive Jewish use of the site.

The closure comes days after Israeli forces ended a 10 day siege of Hebron that brought hundreds of arrests, 15 home demolitions and the displacement of more than 3,300 Palestinians. Settlers have steadily expanded their presence in the Old City, seizing properties and planting new outposts under military protection. The dual holy site remains one of the most sensitive flashpoints in the West Bank.

title: Russia's Ukraine advances shrink to a crawl as diesel cargoes go unsold
summary: Open source maps show only a tiny strip of land taken this year while Ukrainian strikes on refineries and legal risks leave Trump linked diesel shipments without buyers.
body:
Russia's battlefield gains in Ukraine have fallen close to nothing this year even as Moscow pours troops into the fight and steps up strikes on energy infrastructure.

The Institute for the Study of War, which tracks front lines with open source footage, puts territory seized by Russian forces in the first 10 months of 2026 at about 117 square kilometres. That compares with more than 5,300 square kilometres in 2025 and about 3,600 in 2024. The daily advance rate has dropped to a fraction of a square kilometre, down from double digit figures in the previous two years.

Ukraine's General Staff estimates Russian personnel killed or seriously wounded from January through October at more than 381,000, with monthly loss figures breaking wartime records through the summer and autumn. Those claims cannot be independently verified, but the reported toll far exceeds estimates of Russia's monthly recruitment capacity. Assessments also show Moscow losing both firmly held and contested ground in September and October after earlier periods of infiltration.

Ukrainian leaders say the stalled advance helps explain a surge in long range strikes on power infrastructure. In the week ending 6 November Russia launched more than 2,300 drones and over 80 missiles, with a peak of 370 drones and 76 missiles on 3 November. Hundreds of thousands of families face blackouts as winter begins.

At the same time Ukraine has resumed near daily hits on Russian refineries, striking eight in seven days. The campaign aims to cut export revenue and disrupt a late October understanding in which Trump invited Russia to sell 1.8 million tonnes of diesel by year end to ease transport prices. Four tankers were reportedly loaded in hope of US linked sales, but shippers and traders have been wary of sanctions law. A US senator warned one operator that only Congress could make such a sale legally solid. The Kremlin has dismissed reports that the cargoes remain unsold.

title: UN warns millions displaced by Sudan's war risk losing emergency shelter
summary: Agencies say only about one in ten of the 15.4 million people who need shelter support can be reached as warehouses empty and funding dries up.
body:
Millions of people uprooted by Sudan's civil war risk being left without emergency shelter as humanitarian funding and stockpiles run low, United Nations agencies have warned.

The UN refugee agency and the International Organization for Migration said about 15.4 million people across Sudan urgently need emergency shelter and basic household items. Funding shortages mean partners can prioritise help for only about 10 percent of those in need. So far only around 936,000 people have received assistance, leaving a vast gap between need and supply.

In a joint statement on Friday the agencies said they were working with local partners to keep shared supply lines open, pre position stocks in priority areas and deliver aid where the need is greatest. They stressed those efforts cannot continue without predictable and flexible funding.

War between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces since 2023 has created the world's largest displacement crisis. About 8.6 million people are displaced inside Sudan and more than 4.6 million have fled across borders. More than 5.2 million people have also returned to home areas, often finding houses, infrastructure and basic services destroyed.

From Khartoum, the IOM chief in Sudan said warehouses that distributed more than 40,000 tonnes of supplies this year are now completely empty. He warned that internal displacement could rise again despite recent returns and said agencies had already scaled back plans because money is short. Officials argued that a safe place to sleep and basic household goods are the first step toward safety and dignity for families repeatedly forced to move, especially women and children at heightened risk.

title: Yemen sides trade blame after deadly market strike in Taiz kills dozens
summary: Government forces and the Houthis each accuse the other of hitting the al Hadara market as fighting intensifies over a district that commands the Red Sea coast.
body:
Yemen's internationally recognised government forces and the Houthi movement are trading blame for an attack on the al Hadara market in Taiz governorate that both sides say killed and wounded dozens of civilians.

A government military spokesman said Houthi fighters struck the market on Friday with ballistic missiles and called the toll a war crime. Houthi authorities in Sanaa countered that Saudi led aircraft flew three raids on the market, killing at least 30 people and injuring eight, and demanded an independent international inquiry. The competing claims could not be independently verified and there was no immediate public response from the Saudi led coalition.

The market sits in the al Waziiya district, an area held by the Houthis where fighting has been fierce. Local reporting said the Saudi backed campaign is pushing daily to take the district and its mountain range because whoever holds it commands much of the western Red Sea coastal strip.

Government forces said they recaptured several pockets in Taiz on Friday, including villages and stretches of the Sanamat and Ribat al Qarn areas, and tightened sieges on approaches to al Sarari. While the Houthis control much of the wider governorate, Taiz city remains in government hands. A Houthi siege of the city is in its 30th day and the United Nations has warned of a deepening crisis as food and medicine grow scarce for hundreds of thousands of residents.

The recognised government launched Operation Dawn of Yemen on 5 October to claw back Houthi held ground. Since then Houthi missiles and drones have struck Saudi territory almost daily, hitting oil facilities and disrupting air traffic even as coalition and government units press the western front.

title: Settlers seize Palestinian homes in Jericho and force dozens to flee
summary: Eight properties were taken in the West Bank city, with residents reporting gunfire, beatings and stone attacks as families were driven out.
body:
Israeli settlers have forced dozens of Palestinians from their homes in Jericho after seizing eight properties in the West Bank city.

Accounts of the raid describe settlers firing live ammunition, beating residents and throwing stones as families were driven out. The seizures add to a pattern of settler expansion into Palestinian neighbourhoods under the protection of Israeli security forces.

Jericho sits deep in the Jordan Valley and has long been a focus of pressure on Palestinian communities. Local residents say the latest takeover leaves households without shelter and deepens fear that further properties will be targeted. Rights groups and Palestinian officials regularly warn that such seizures, often followed by outposts or permanent settler presence, entrench displacement far from the main headlines of the conflict.

The Jericho incidents come amid wider unrest across the West Bank, including restrictions at holy sites in Hebron and ongoing demolitions elsewhere. Families displaced in Jericho now face the immediate task of finding shelter while seeking legal and political recourse that rarely reverses settler takeovers once they are established.

title: Senior US Justice Department officials resign after Democratic midterm sweep
summary: A Florida US attorney known for Trump backed probes and the head of the national security division quit as the administration braces for congressional investigations.
body:
Two more senior figures have left the United States Justice Department in the wake of the Democratic midterm victory, extending an exodus of Trump aligned officials.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said Jason Reding Quinones, the US attorney for the Southern District of Florida, submitted his resignation on Friday. Quinones had overseen and expanded a federal probe into Russia's alleged role around the 2016 election, a case Trump has long cast as a political witch hunt even after a special investigator found no direct collusion with his campaign. Critics say the department pursued politically charged investigations at the president's urging.

The Florida office's work reportedly included subpoenas aimed at former intelligence chiefs, though no charges followed from that line of inquiry. Separately, former FBI director James Comey has faced charging efforts that he calls an abuse of the department. Quinones also oversaw the indictment of elderly Cuban revolutionary Raul Castro as part of a wider pressure campaign on Havana. Blanche praised his record on violent crime, trafficking and transnational cases.

On the same day John Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for the national security division, also resigned. Blanche said he had strengthened the response to foreign and domestic threats. The departures follow the exit of Harmeet Dhillon, who led the civil rights division and faced fierce criticism over its direction.

The wave of resignations lands as Trump officials prepare for Democrat led oversight once the new Congress convenes. Control of the House and Senate will give Democrats subpoena power, and several inquiries are expected to focus on alleged politicisation of the Justice Department.

title: Dozens of Democrats already eye 2028 White House run after midterm wins
summary: A former Obama campaign chief says more than twenty campaigns are hiring staff and raising money, with exploratory committees expected soon after Thanksgiving.
body:
More than two dozen Democrats are already weighing White House bids for 2028 after the party's sweeping midterm gains, according to Jim Messina, who ran Barack Obama's 2012 re election campaign.

Messina said he has spoken to over twenty campaigns that are actively exploring a run, starting the financing process and hiring staff. He expects exploratory committees to be announced in the coming weeks, likely after Thanksgiving. He said he already knows of someone relocating to work on a governor's presidential effort.

He predicted the field will shrink once candidates face the fundraising demands of a primary calendar. In private talks he presses hopefuls on their economic vision and their plans for artificial intelligence. He also warned that Trump will still be in office during the campaign season, forcing Democrats to choose whether to answer him every day or stay on their own message.

Messina credited the midterm success to a disciplined focus on the economy and the impact of tariffs, which he said hit rural voters hard through higher fuel and living costs. That message, he argued, helped flip seats in traditionally Republican states such as Iowa, Kansas and Texas. He said Democrats for once refused to be drawn into culture fights and stuck to kitchen table concerns.

He cautioned that the result was not a broad endorsement of the party and called Trump the unlikely most valuable player of the election for Democrats. The harder task now, he said, will be holding progressive and centrist wings together in Congress while a crowded bench of governors and senators tests the waters for 2028. Names already gaining attention after strong midterm showings include Georgia senator Jon Ossoff and Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro, though neither has declared.

title: European forces drill for a possible post ceasefire mission in Ukraine
summary: French and British led exercises in Poland will test how fast about 2,800 troops from ten countries could deploy if fighting stops.
body:
European militaries are practising how they would move into Ukraine if a ceasefire takes hold, with French and British led drills in Poland focused on speed of deployment.

About 2,800 troops from ten European countries are involved in the exercises, which are designed to show whether a multinational force could arrive quickly after any halt in fighting. Planners are treating the scenario as a contingency rather than a signal that a deal is imminent.

The training comes as diplomatic talk of a broader settlement continues in Washington and European capitals, while combat on the ground shows little sign of a lasting pause. Kyiv has long sought stronger security guarantees from European partners, and capitals that back Ukraine want reassurance they could act together if asked to help police a future truce.

Officials frame the Poland drills as preparation, not a commitment to send combat troops into an active war. Even so, the visible rehearsal underscores how seriously European governments are planning for the day after a ceasefire, including logistics, command links and the political hurdle of putting soldiers on Ukrainian soil with Moscow still armed nearby.

title: Providence voters back city move to divest from Israel linked holdings
summary: About three quarters of ballots in the Rhode Island city favoured an ordinance telling officials to drop investments tied to what campaigners call genocide and apartheid.
body:
Voters in Providence, Rhode Island, have approved an ordinance calling on the city to end investments that support Israel in terms campaigners describe as genocide and apartheid.

About 75 percent of those who cast ballots backed the measure, an emphatic local result that advocates cast as part of a wider shift toward pro Palestine politics in parts of the United States. The vote instructs city officials to unwind holdings tied to the targeted categories, though the practical timeline for any sell off will depend on how the ordinance is implemented and on existing financial contracts.

Supporters say municipal money should not underwrite occupation or military campaigning in Gaza and the West Bank. Opponents typically argue that such divestment singles out one country, harms pension returns, or oversimplifies a complex conflict. Similar debates have played out on US campuses and in other city councils, but a three to one margin in a state capital vote gives the Providence result unusual weight as a signal of changing Democratic and progressive voter sentiment after years of war coverage.

City lawyers and finance officers must now translate the ballot win into concrete portfolio changes. How fast Providence acts, and whether other US cities follow, will determine whether the vote remains a symbolic milestone or the start of a broader municipal divestment wave.

title: Ukraine raises death toll from Zaporizhia aid centre strike above 50
summary: Rescuers say Monday's bombing of a village aid site is among the deadliest Russian attacks this year, with dozens still feared under the rubble.
body:
Ukraine has raised the death toll from a Russian strike on an aid distribution centre in the Zaporizhia region to more than 50, calling it one of the deadliest attacks of the year.

Emergency crews said Friday that more bodies had been recovered from the ruins in the village of Komyshuvakha after Monday's raid. The acting regional governor put the toll at 53 as searchers worked into a fifth day. Local police earlier listed dozens of people as missing and warned that many may still lie trapped under debris.

Ukrainian officials say Russian aircraft bombed a former school near the front that civilians used for weekly aid handouts. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a first blast was followed by a second wave aimed at the underground shelter where people had taken cover, causing most of the destruction. Police officers and rescue workers were among the dead.

DNA testing is being used to identify remains while further Russian fire continues to endanger the rescue effort. The United Nations human rights mission in Ukraine said the strike was likely a breach of international law. Kyiv cast the attack as proof that Moscow will not halt the fighting even after short local pauses elsewhere along the line.

The raid came a day after a brief ceasefire ended in a Russian occupied city further south. For families still waiting on names and for communities that rely on aid points near the front, the rising toll underlines how civilian supply lines remain exposed in a war now stretching toward its fifth year.

title: Europe fears a US security deal with Russia that weakens NATO
summary: Officials worry Washington could strike terms with Moscow that restore a Russian sphere of influence and undercut allied security guarantees.
body:
European governments are sounding the alarm over reports that Washington is exploring a security arrangement with Moscow that allies fear could hollow out NATO and hand Russia a renewed sphere of influence.

Public briefings from European officials describe anxiety that any bilateral understanding between the United States and Russia might trade Ukrainian leverage or eastern flank guarantees for a quick diplomatic win. Capitals that have poured weapons and money into Ukraine's defence say they were not reassured by signals that the White House wants a grand bargain with the Kremlin.

The concern lands days after Democratic midterm gains, when many in Europe hoped Congress would stiffen American support. Diplomats note that foreign policy still runs chiefly through the presidency, so legislative shifts may not block a deal if the White House pursues one.

Allies are pressing for consultation before any text takes shape and for clear red lines on Ukrainian sovereignty and forward defence of NATO members. Without that, they warn, years of military aid and political unity could be spent down in a settlement that freezes the war on Moscow's preferred map.

title: Trump weighs vetoes and deals after Democrats take Congress
summary: With both chambers lost, the president says he will not spend two years only blocking bills, even as he flaunts the veto power he still holds.
body:
President Donald Trump is weighing how to govern after Democrats seized both chambers of Congress, floating cooperation even while reminding rivals that he can veto nearly anything they pass.

As midterm results confirmed a Democratic wave, Trump told an interviewer he had already taken calls from Democrats who want to work with him. He said he does not want to spend two years only striking down legislation, while stressing that the veto remains his. He later posted imagery playing on the word veto, underlining the leverage he still holds.

Democrats have secured comfortable majorities in the House and Senate on the counts reported so far, yet they lack the two thirds margins needed to override a presidential veto in either chamber. Analysts say that leaves three broad paths for the White House: veto bills, lean harder on executive orders, or cut selective deals.

Trump has already signed hundreds of executive orders across his current term, a habit that may grow if Capitol Hill turns hostile. Scholars of American politics expect stretches of gridlock, with Democrats advancing priorities they know may die on his desk and the president picking moments to bargain when he wants a win.

For markets, allies and domestic agencies, the practical question is which files invite compromise and which invite confrontation. Immigration, spending, artificial intelligence rules and foreign military authorities all sit in the contested middle. The midterms changed the arithmetic; they did not remove the veto pen.

title: US tech shares rebound after midterm AI selloff
summary: The Nasdaq climbed in Friday trade as chipmakers clawed back part of Thursday's steep losses tied to fears of slower AI growth under Democrats.
body:
United States technology shares bounced on Friday after a bruising midterm selloff that had wiped trillions from market values on worries that Democratic gains would slow the artificial intelligence boom.

The Nasdaq Composite opened more than one percent higher and kept rising in early trade, reversing part of Thursday's drop of about five and a half percent. The S&P 500 also edged up while the Dow was little changed. Chip and AI linked names that led the plunge led the repair job.

Nvidia, which had shed hundreds of billions in value after a slide of more than nine percent, jumped more than six percent at the open. AMD and Micron, both down more than seventeen percent on Thursday, posted strong double digit percentage gains in early Friday dealing. Tesla and other previously hit names showed smaller recoveries.

Investors had sold technology stocks partly because they expect a Democratic Congress to tighten rules on data centres, power use and AI buildouts. Fresh employment figures that showed a surprisingly firm hiring print added to a mixed macro picture and helped some buyers step back in.

The rebound does not erase Thursday's damage or settle the policy debate. Traders are still parsing how far new majorities will go on AI scrutiny, export controls and energy permits. For now the message from the tape is simpler: part of the panic faded once bargain hunters returned to the same chip giants that led the rout.

title: US employers add 165,000 jobs in stronger than forecast report
summary: A hiring rebound led by professional services pointed to continued strength in the American labour market after the midterm shock.
body:
United States employers added 165,000 jobs in the latest monthly report, outstripping forecasts and underscoring resilience in the American labour market even as politics and markets jolted after the midterms.

Hiring strength was led by professional services, according to the public summary of the figures, painting a firmer picture than many economists had expected. The print landed on a morning when technology shares were trying to rebound from a steep AI linked selloff and investors were hunting for signals on growth and interest rate paths.

A solid jobs number complicates simple narratives that political upheaval would immediately cool the economy. It also feeds debate at the Federal Reserve about how much room remains to adjust borrowing costs while unemployment stays contained and pay pressures evolve.

For the White House and the new Democratic majorities on Capitol Hill, the data offer a backdrop of still functioning labour demand as budget and regulatory fights begin. For workers, the headline is more direct: employers kept adding roles at a pace that beat the consensus screen.

title: Iran's chief negotiator says Americans voted no to war
summary: Parliament speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf hailed the midterm message against the conflict as Trump again tied Republican losses to the Iran fight and higher fuel prices.
body:
Iran's chief negotiator with the United States says American voters delivered a clear no to war, after Republicans suffered heavy midterm losses that President Donald Trump partly blamed on the Iran conflict.

Parliament speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf wrote that Americans had voted against the war and that Tehran endorsed that message. He warned that if Washington ignored its own public to serve what he called foreign paymasters, Iran's refusal would come with severe consequences.

Trump has acknowledged that the fighting and the jump in petrol prices hurt Republican candidates, while insisting he does not regret launching the campaign and saying the war ends when he decides it ends. In recent weeks he has also left open the chance of renewed all out strikes with Israel if no deal is reached.

The exchange captures the strange symmetry of the moment. Iranian officials cast the ballot box as proof that the war is unpopular in America. The White House still claims authority to continue or expand operations. Mediators and markets are left reading both the vote and the threats as they wait for the next concrete proposal or the next raid.

title: Ukraine arrests woman behind viral false conscription torture claim
summary: Officials say a staged rescue outside Kyiv fuelled a global storm over draft tactics, after a crowd stormed a suburban house on false allegations.
body:
Ukrainian authorities have arrested a woman who sparked a viral scandal by claiming men seized for conscription were being tortured in a suburban house outside Kyiv, officials say the episode was staged.

Valentyna Moloda, described as a 49 year old nurse not authorised to work as a paramedic, knelt before police at a two storey house in Petropavlivska Borshchagivka and alleged that armed captors were holding dozens of draft evaders, with at least one already dead. An ambulance marked with logos of a private firm said to have closed years earlier stood nearby as a companion livestreamed and a crowd swelled into the hundreds.

Protesters threw eggs and tomatoes, clashed with officers into the night and pushed a narrative that spread worldwide among critics of Ukraine's draft. Conscription teams are widely disliked for harsh methods, which helped the claim catch fire before facts caught up.

Officials now say the rescue was fake and prepared in advance. Ukraine's intelligence leadership said Moloda and a driver had scouted the property days earlier. Investigators argue the house was not a torture site and that the performance was built to inflame.

The affair leaves a double wound. It exposed raw anger over how men are pulled into a grinding war with Russia. It also showed how quickly an unverified livestream can shape foreign perceptions of a country fighting for survival. Courts and police will now test the fraud case while commanders still face a public that distrusts the draft.

title: Uncertainty grips Iran after US midterm shock
summary: Pro government crowds celebrate Republican losses while many Iranians fear repression will continue whatever happens next with Trump and the war.
body:
Hours after Republican losses in the US midterms became clear, crowds in Tehran burned a giant banner showing Donald Trump, JD Vance, envoy Steve Witkoff and Benjamin Netanyahu. Officials cast the vote as a rebuke of Trump's war on Iran. Supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei said America's decline had sped up. State television even aired a staged mock hanging of Trump.

Away from the rallies, many Iranians describe dread rather than triumph. A Tehran journalist said people feel trapped in a strange limbo, looking to Washington and Jerusalem for change while the economy worsens and daily life grows harsher. Some fear that, with no re election race left for Trump, he could escalate again. Others think another full scale war is less likely after the ballot shock. Almost all agree the security state at home will not ease.

A rights monitor based in Oslo says Iranian authorities have executed at least 696 people this year. Residents speak of shops still open while real purchases shrink, of families debating heaters in case infrastructure is hit again, and of a prison machine that kept running through earlier fighting. A medic in central Iran argued outsiders still underestimate the Revolutionary Guard's loyalty and competence, and that a system able to absorb sanctions can also turn that force on its own people.

The mood on the street is preparation for the worst with little faith that European leaders will press the case of those still being arrested and killed. Celebrations by hardliners, one resident said, look like relief that the ruling structure has found room to survive.

title: Saudi led strike on Yemeni home kills nine relatives, family says
summary: Relatives say an October air raid destroyed a household in the war against the Houthis, renewing focus on civilian deaths in the US backed campaign.
body:
Relatives say a Saudi led air raid in October destroyed a Yemeni home and killed nine members of one family, spotlighting civilian harm in the long campaign against the Houthis.

The strike is described as part of operations that also involve US support. Families and local accounts place the dead inside a residential building rather than a clear military site, a pattern rights monitors have flagged across years of fighting in Yemen.

Riyadh and its partners cast the air war as necessary to roll back Houthi advances and protect shipping and border areas. Critics say too little is done to verify targets or account for households caught under the bombs.

The fresh allegations land while Yemen's recognised government has been reshuffling ministers and officers after Houthi gains, and while southern factions press for a larger share of power. Independent confirmation of every casualty claim is hard in active war zones, but the family's account adds to pressure for clearer rules of engagement and public investigations when homes are hit.

title: Ukraine greets US midterm blow to Trump with cautious hope
summary: Democratic gains raise talk of a harder line in peace talks as Russia's war on Ukraine nears its fifth year.
body:
In Ukraine, the Democratic surge in the US midterms has mixed guarded optimism with dark humour about what comes next for a war drifting toward its fifth year.

Many officials and analysts think a Congress less aligned with Donald Trump could stiffen American support and change the leverage in any peace track with Moscow. Others warn that foreign policy still sits heavily with the White House, so battlefield aid and diplomacy may shift only slowly.

Kyiv has spent months reading every signal from Washington on weapons, sanctions and talks involving Kremlin envoys. A weaker Republican hand on Capitol Hill is seen as room to argue for sustained pressure on Russia rather than a rapid deal that freezes lines on Moscow's terms.

Nothing about the vote ends the fighting. Russian strikes continue and Ukrainian forces still need munitions, air defence and money. But for a public exhausted by attrition, the midterm map is being read as a possible brake on any rush to settle on unfavourable ground.

title: Europe still sees Trump as decisive on Ukraine Iran and NATO
summary: Democratic midterm wins bring private relief in some capitals, yet leaders expect the White House to keep steering the hardest foreign files.
body:
European governments are treating the Democratic midterm wave as important but not decisive for the wars and alliances that matter most to them.

Private relief is real in some ministries that feared unchecked Republican control would shrink support for Ukraine or unsettle NATO planning. Official glee is scarce. Diplomats note that Donald Trump still runs foreign policy day to day, including files on Ukraine, Iran and the future of the alliance.

Capitals are gaming out how a hostile Congress might constrain spending, appointments and sanctions while the president courts bilateral deals. Ukraine's ammunition needs, Iran contingency planning after months of strikes, and burden sharing inside NATO all still run through White House choices more than committee rooms.

The working assumption in many European briefings is continuity with sharper legislative friction, not a sudden handoff of strategy. Allies will keep talking to both parties, hedge their own defence budgets, and watch whether midterm politics hardens or softens America's next moves abroad.

title: Musk says Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production next year
summary: The company plans to free Texas factory space for driverless Cybercab builds after years of delays and weak Cybertruck sales.
body:
Elon Musk says Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas plant next year to make room for more Cybercab robotaxis. He did not say whether the angular pickup would vanish entirely or move elsewhere, but the project's lead engineer wrote that the truck lived on through the Cybercab.

The vehicle won a loyal fan base yet arrived late in 2023 after long delays and has posted soft sales against hopes for America's truck market. Musk still calls it among Tesla's best products and told mourners online that the existing fleet will last for years, while agreeing the line is ending.

Public memory still includes the 2019 launch stunt when advertised unbreakable glass shattered on stage. Pre orders once looked huge; demand in showrooms never matched the myth. Shifting space toward unsupervised robotaxis fits Musk's bet that autonomy, not niche trucks, will define the next chapter.

Workers, suppliers and owners now wait for a clearer end date and for whether any Cybertruck work continues outside Texas. For Tesla the message is strategic: scarce factory capacity goes to the product Wall Street is being asked to value next.

title: West Bank settlement dates sold in Australia as produce of Israel
summary: Trade analysis finds millions of dollars of organic dates from illegal settlements shipped to Australia under an Israel origin label.
body:
Millions of dollars of food grown in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank has reached Australia labelled as produce of Israel, according to a new review of trade papers.

Researchers at the rights group Global Echo examined commercial documents and official statistics and say at least five million US dollars of organic dates from settlements moved to Australia over eight years. Of 132 agricultural shipments from Israel studied between 2018 and 2026, 85 contained settlement goods. In 2025 and early 2026 the share was higher still, with most date consignments tied to settlement farms.

Sites named in the work include Netiv Hagdud, Beit Haarava, Arvot Jericho, Hamra, Tomer, Mechora and Naaran, areas Australia recognises as part of Palestine. Israeli rules generally require exports from settlements to be marked as Israeli unless the destination bans that practice. Australia has no ban on settlement imports and no rule forcing labels that show occupied origin.

Foreign minister Penny Wong has called the settlements illegal and urged Israel to rein in settler violence, while resisting a blanket import ban over worries for Australian firms. Campaigners say shoppers buying Israeli labelled dates may still be funding the settlement economy, and that unclear origin marking is a pattern also seen on routes into Europe.

title: Silicon Valley elites rethink politics after midterm backlash
summary: AI executives and tech donors who aligned with Donald Trump are plotting a new political strategy after that wager soured at the ballot box.
body:
Silicon Valley elites and artificial intelligence executives are redrawing their political playbook after an alliance with Donald Trump backfired in the midterm elections.

Heavy campaign spending and public alignment with the White House failed to deliver the outcomes many founders and investors sought. Voters in key races punished candidates tied to tech money and to the costs of the AI buildout, leaving donors who bet on Trump facing a Congress and state houses less friendly to unconstrained data centre expansion.

Industry figures now talk of quieter lobbying, broader bipartisan outreach and messaging that softens the industry's association with one party. Some want to stress jobs and innovation rather than culture war fights; others simply want to avoid becoming the face of another losing ticket.

The recalibration matters because AI capital and chip supply chains still depend on federal permits, power policy and export rules. After the midterms, political permission looks scarcer than venture funding. How quickly Valley leaders can rebuild credibility with both parties will shape the next round of regulation and the industry's social licence to keep building at speed.

title: Herzog to name coalition candidate by Sunday after Eisenkot leads endorsements
summary: Sixty seven lawmakers backed former military chief Gadi Eisenkot against 46 for Benjamin Netanyahu, but Israel's president says mutual vetoes still cloud who can actually form a government.
body:
Israel's president Isaac Herzog says he will name a candidate to form the next government by Sunday, after a majority of lawmakers endorsed opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Herzog spoke on Thursday after marathon consultations with parties elected to the 120 seat Knesset. Some 67 lawmakers recommended Eisenkot, a former military chief, while 46 backed Netanyahu. In televised remarks he cautioned that although the consultation numbers look clear, mutual vetoes between and within blocs make it hard to say who has the best chance of assembling a stable coalition. He plans further personal talks with party leaders over the Israeli weekend and a decision on Sunday.

October's election left neither camp with an obvious majority. Netanyahu's Likud took the most seats of any single party with 27, yet his wider religious nationalist coalition finished on 53. Eisenkot's alliance of four Jewish led parties spanning centre left to right won 48. Two parties representing Israel's Palestinian minority together took a record 19 seats.

Eisenkot, like Netanyahu, has ruled out a formal government with the Arab led parties. Both of those parties nonetheless recommended him, giving him the endorsement of a comfortable majority of lawmakers. His Yashar party said 67 recommendations were the most any candidate had received since 2015 and urged Herzog to hand him the mandate quickly so he could build a national emergency government.

Netanyahu suffered a further setback when United Torah Judaism, a longtime ultra Orthodox ally, declined to recommend anyone, breaking with him over the failure to pass legislation exempting ultra Orthodox men from military service. Allies of Eisenkot argue that party's support could still be won with the right offer, leaving Netanyahu with little realistic path to a majority.

Once nominated, a candidate has 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14 day extension. Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister until a coalition is sworn in or fresh elections are called if every attempt fails. He has seized on an election officials' inquiry into possible vote tampering to cast doubt on the result, accusing Arab led parties of stealing the vote, claims critics say are meant to undermine a defeat he denies.

title: US judge pauses Trump triumphal arch works in Washington DC
summary: District Judge Tanya Chutkan ordered a 14 day halt on the roughly 76 metre arch project after planning commissioners approved it over strong public opposition.
body:
A United States federal judge has ordered a temporary block on construction of President Donald Trump's planned triumphal arch in Washington DC.

US District Judge Tanya Chutkan on Friday imposed a 14 day pause on any work on the roughly 250 foot (76 metre) structure, even though the administration had said building could start as soon as Thursday. The National Capital Planning Commission held a nine hour hearing the day before and voted 8 to 4 to approve the arch despite dozens of witnesses who opposed it.

Lawsuits challenging the project include one filed in February by a group of Vietnam war veterans. Trump has proposed siting the arch near Arlington National Cemetery, prompting concern that it could interrupt the carefully designed line of sight between the cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. Veterans argued in court papers that the vista was meant to symbolise national unity after the Civil War.

Trump first floated the arch last year to mark 250 years of US independence, comparing it to famous European arches such as the Arc de Triomphe in Paris. Critics have mocked the scheme as an Arc de Trump. It is one of several Washington projects he has pushed; on Friday he also signed a proclamation designating the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as a national monument.

Many of his capital plans have already been blocked by judges. After Democrats won control of Congress in this week's midterms, further projects are expected to face sharper scrutiny. For now the arch sits under a short court pause while litigation continues.

title: Israel tightens rules on Palestinian schools in East Jerusalem
summary: Around 180 teachers face the loss of entry permits when they expire at the end of the 2026 to 27 academic year, while funding for new schools is tied to adopting the Israeli curriculum.
body:
Palestinian education in East Jerusalem is under mounting pressure as Israel restricts teacher entry permits and links school funding to adoption of the Israeli curriculum.

About 180 Palestinian teachers have been told their travel permits into East Jerusalem will not be renewed when they expire at the end of the 2026 to 27 academic year. Many commute daily from the occupied West Bank through Israeli checkpoints. Even when permits are issued they are tightly limited by hours and location: holders may not exceed set times, may not go anywhere except the school, and since the Gaza war began in 2023 have been barred from accompanying students on trips or visiting Al Aqsa for prayer.

Permit delays already disrupted this year. Documents arrived only on 15 September, two weeks after term began, and similar delays in January triggered school strikes meant to show a united front. Teachers were also blocked from entering Jerusalem for a full week during the recent Jewish holiday of Sukkot.

Wider policies sit under a government plan framed as reducing socioeconomic gaps in East Jerusalem, whose population remains majority Palestinian despite settlement growth. Roughly half the education budget under that plan goes toward expanding teaching of the Israeli curriculum. New state funded schools must adopt that curriculum as a condition of opening, which rights monitors describe as pressure on schools and parents to abandon the Palestinian programme. Teacher training inside the Israeli education system is being expanded alongside those incentives.

An Israeli human rights organisation, Ir Amim, has warned that the measures exploit genuine educational needs to erode Palestinian educational autonomy and national identity. A separate law barring employment of teachers with degrees from Palestinian universities is expected to deepen an already severe staffing shortage.

East Jerusalem, like the West Bank, is occupied Palestinian territory under international law, though Israel treats it as part of a unified capital under its control. Teachers who have spent decades crossing checkpoints say the latest permit cuts may finally force them out of classrooms they have staffed for years, accelerating a shift toward Israeli supervised schooling in the eastern half of the city.

title: Lebanese stock food and pack bags amid fears of another Israeli push
summary: Residents who lived through earlier rounds of fighting say drones and detonations never fully stopped, and many are preparing for a possible third intensification since 2024.
body:
Lebanese families who endured earlier Israeli offensives are stocking medicine and food, charging devices and packing bags as fears grow of another escalation in the south.

A ceasefire announced in April eased the heaviest fighting after a surge of attacks that killed hundreds in a short span, yet residents say drones and distant detonations remain part of daily life. In recent weeks worry has sharpened around a potential third Israeli intensification since 2024, especially among people who lived through the autumn 2024 and March to April 2026 campaigns.

One woman from Abbasiyeh in southern Lebanon said her family prepared extra medication for her grandparents in case a new round makes supplies hard to reach. She stayed through the March intensification even when a neighbour's house was hit, but now says she would leave rather than endure another displacement. Others keep go bags ready and electronics charged should strikes resume.

Hezbollah and Israel have been at war since October 2023. Lebanese health authorities put the death toll in Lebanon at around 9,000, mostly during the major escalations. Israel invaded during each offensive and has since held territory up to about 10 kilometres inside Lebanon behind what it calls a Yellow Line, continuing demolition of towns and villages below that line and leaving border areas barely habitable.

A US brokered framework agreed in June sketched pilot zones in which Israeli forces would pull back and the Lebanese army would move in to disarm Hezbollah. Active fighting has eased since then, though Israel continues attacks and destruction in the far south. People living above the Yellow Line are mostly outside the heaviest fire but still hear constant explosions and drones and sometimes struggle to reach their land.

Reports that Washington has considered another round of strikes on Iran, coordinated with Israel, have raised questions about whether Hezbollah might resume its own attacks. Israeli officials have also accused the Lebanese army of failing its part of the framework deal, a charge the army denies. Analysts say such claims can serve as political cover for a fresh bombing campaign. For residents, the practical response is simpler: pack, stock up, and decide whether to stay or go if the sky lights up again.

title: Satellite images point to major building work near Iran missile sites
summary: Analysts say November imagery shows digging and new structures at bases near Tehran and further north, plus repairs at other military complexes hit in earlier US and Israeli strikes.
body:
Satellite imagery from November points to major new construction and repair work near Iranian missile facilities, according to analysts who reviewed the photographs.

Digging and fresh buildings are visible at the Garmdareh military base in Karaj near Tehran and at the Shahroud base in the north. A British intelligence firm, MAIAR, examined the pictures and described the activity as significant. Separate imagery suggests repair work at at least a dozen other military sites, including missile complexes and air bases.

At Kermanshah in western Iran, near the Iraqi border, new roofs appear on buildings previously destroyed. At the Parchin complex east of the capital, damaged structures and debris have been cleared. Analysts also say substantial work has been finished at the Taleghan 2 facility inside Parchin, with damaged buildings levelled and an underground bunker reinforced with concrete after earlier attacks.

Excavation near Shahroud may relate to missile production, a former CIA analyst focused on Iran told reviewers. Because the nearby air base has been struck repeatedly in recent years, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps is likely seeking ways to shift production underground. A MAIAR analyst said Iran has a pattern of moving infrastructure below ground to shield it from further strikes. Defence analysts note that underground sites also make it harder for outside observers to judge how much capacity remains intact.

At Karaj, vehicles appear in the imagery and improvements seem under way at the nearby air base. One research analyst described what looks like a new portal for an underground facility. An intelligence firm analyst argued the work is unlikely to be staged merely to deceive foreign agencies, calling such a project costly for little gain.

The pictures land after White House claims that US and Israeli strikes heavily depleted Iranian forces, including Pentagon assertions that much of Iran's drone, ballistic missile and naval industrial base was destroyed. Tehran insists it still holds large missile stockpiles, and state television this week aired footage it said showed dozens of missiles at the entrance to an underground facility in southern Iran.

Speculation has grown that Washington could resume attacks after this week's midterms, though Vice President JD Vance linked the war's unpopularity with voters to the Republicans' weak showing and possible loss of Senate control.

title: Trump declares the Oval Office a national monument
summary: President Donald Trump has signed an executive order making the Oval Office and some nearby rooms a national monument, aiming to lock in his gold heavy redesign and the East Wing ballroom works against later presidents.
body:
President Donald Trump has signed an executive order declaring the Oval Office, and some surrounding rooms, a national monument in a bid to stop future presidents from undoing his changes to the West Wing.

The move follows a highly visible redesign that filled the Oval Office with gold accents and a broader project that tore into the East Wing to make space for a large ballroom. Critics have already challenged parts of that building work in court, and Congress never gave a clear green light for the scale of the renovation. By wrapping the rooms in monument status, the White House is trying to raise the legal bar for anyone who wants to strip the decor back out.

The order is not an absolute freeze. It still lets a sitting president redecorate, swap furnishings and make security modifications so long as those changes do not substantially impair the historic structure. In practice that leaves room for taste and security upgrades while aiming to block a wholesale reversal of Trump's imprint.

Monument designations are normally used for landscapes, battlefields and cultural sites of lasting public value. Applying the tool to working rooms inside the White House is unusual and will invite fresh lawsuits from preservation groups and political opponents who say the president is using heritage law as a shield for personal style.

Allies cast the order as protection for a restored grandeur they say visitors and history will remember. Detractors call it an attempt to constitutionalise one administration's aesthetic after midterm losses that already weaken Trump's hand with Congress.

The practical test will come later. A future president who wants a plainer Oval Office will have to argue that new furnishings or a different colour scheme leave the historic fabric intact, or else spend political capital trying to unwind the designation. For now the public facts are clear enough: the Oval Office and named adjoining spaces sit under a new monument order, the ballroom project remains contested, and the White House insists day to day working changes are still allowed.

title: Iran security chief meets Putin and delivers a letter from Mojtaba Khamenei
summary: Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei has met Vladimir Putin in Moscow and handed over a message from Mojtaba Khamenei. Talks covered regional security, post war arrangements and plans for Russian gas pipelines into Iran.
body:
Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei has met President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and delivered a written message from Mojtaba Khamenei, deepening a wartime channel between Tehran and the Kremlin.

Public accounts of the visit say the agenda spanned regional security, arrangements after the fighting and energy cooperation, including ideas for gas pipelines that would carry Russian supply into Iran.
